question: During resuscitation of a 2-year-old child in cardiac arrest, two attempts at peripheral IV cannulation fail within 90 seconds. The team decides to establish intraosseous (IO) access. Which of the following best describes the PREFERRED primary site for IO insertion in young children?

answers.text: Distal tibia, 1–2 cm above the medial malleolus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The distal tibia (1–2 cm above the medial malleolus) is a valid alternative IO site and is preferred in older children and adolescents where the proximal tibial cortex may be thicker. In young children (under 6 years), the proximal tibia is the primary preferred site.

answers.text: Proximal tibia, 1–2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity on the flat medial surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In young children, the proximal tibia — specifically the flat medial surface 1–2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity — is the preferred primary IO site. The cortex is flat, accessible, and away from the growth plate. IO access provides immediate entry into the bone marrow sinusoid, which drains into the central venous circulation, allowing delivery of all resuscitation drugs and fluids at comparable systemic concentrations to IV.

The femoral neck is not an IO access site. IO insertion uses the flat cortical surfaces of long bones (proximal/distal tibia, distal femur, humeral head in adults). The femoral neck approach would be anatomically incorrect and dangerous.

answers.text: Iliac crest, 2 cm posterior to the anterior superior iliac spine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The iliac crest can be used in adults and older adolescents but is not the preferred IO site in young children. The proximal tibia offers a larger, more accessible flat cortical surface in this age group, and is the standard first choice in paediatric resuscitation guidelines.

overallFeedback.feedback: The preferred primary IO site in young children is the proximal tibia — the flat medial surface just below and medial to the tibial tuberosity, safely away from the growth plate. Review the IO anatomy section before attempting simulated insertion.

Correct. In young children, the proximal tibia (1–2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity) is the standard first-choice IO site. IO access is indicated when peripheral IV fails after 2 attempts or 90 seconds in a life-threatening emergency.
